1000092.etyen:
Internationalism, based ultimately on Romanian România (“Romania”). The Romanian name is formed from român (“Romanian”) and -ia, the definite form of -ie. The ethnonym român is inherited from Latin Latin Rōmānus (“Roman”), from Rōma (“Rome”).
Parallel international forms include Norwegian Nynorsk Romania, Danish Rumænien, Swedish Rumänien, German Rumänien, Dutch Roemenië, French Roumanie, Italian Romania, Spanish Rumanía, Portuguese Roménia and English Romania (“Romania”).

1000348.etyen:
From russ (“Russian person”) + land (“country, land”), literally “land of the Russians”. The first element is ultimately from Old East Slavic Русь (Rusĭ, “Rus”), borrowed from Proto-Finnic *roocci (“Swedes”), itself borrowed from Old East Norse *rōþs- (“related to rowing”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *rōþruz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“to row”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Russland, Danish Rusland, Swedish Ryssland, Icelandic Rússland, Faroese Russland and German Russland (“Russia”).

1000604.etyen:
From republikken (“the republic”), the definite singular of republikk (“republic”), followed by Kongo (“Kongo”); literally “the Republic of Kongo”. The name corresponds to the country's official French name French République du Congo (“Republic of the Congo”). For the further origin of Kongo, see that entry.
The republic was established as a self-governing entity within the French Community in 1958 and became independent in 1960. It was renamed Folkerepublikken Kongo (“People's Republic of the Congo”) in 1969; the name corresponding to Republikken Kongo was restored in 1991.

x: Før selvstendigheten var Sør-Sudan en del av Sudan.
Before independence, Southern Sudan was part of Sudan.
Sudan ble selvstendig republikk fra 1. januar 1956, og Sør-Sudan ble en integrert landsdel.
Sudan became an independent republic on 1 January 1956, and Southern Sudan became an integral region of the country.

1002396.etyen:
From sør (“south”) + Sudan (“Sudan”), literally “South Sudan”. The name was already used for the southern part of Sudan before that region became the independent state of South Sudan on 9 July 2011.
The first element sør (“south”) continues Old Norse Old Norse suðr (“south”), from Proto-Germanic Proto-Germanic *sunþrą (“south”), ultimately related to Proto-Indo-European Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ (“sun”). The second element Sudan ultimately derives from Arabic سُودَان (sūdān, “black people”), historically occurring in بِلَاد السُّودَان (“land of the Black people”).

en.g: goodbye, bye; used when taking leave of someone
x: Vi snakkes i morgen. Ha det!
mennesker man sa «hei», eller «ha’ det» eller «morn’a» til

1003932.etyen:
Ellipsis of ha det bra (“goodbye, take care”, literally “have it well”). Språkrådet (“The Language Council of Norway”) describes the expression as a shortening of either this phrase or ha det godt (“goodbye, take care”), likewise literally “have it well”. Both fuller expressions are imperative farewell formulas using ha (“to have”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk ha det and Swedish ha det (“goodbye, bye”).

en.g: a female given name from Latin [in turn from Old High German, in turn from Proto-Germanic], equivalent to English Ottilie

1004700.etyen:
One of several Norwegian spellings of a female given name going back to Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, a Latinised form of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda. The Old High German names are formed from the Germanic name element reflected in *audaz (“wealth, riches”), with a pet-name or diminutive ending.
Compare Danish Otilie, Swedish Otilie, German Ottilie and English Ottilie (“female given name”).

en.g: Wing leader; an officer or pilot responsible for tactically leading an aviation wing
x: Han tjenestegjorde som vingleder før han senere ble skvadronsjef.
He served as a wing leader before later becoming a squadron commander.
Deretter var han vingleder frem til 2003, før han ble sjef for 337 skvadronen på Bardufoss
He then served as a wing leader until 2003, before becoming commander of 337 Squadron at Bardufoss.

1004956.etyen:
Formed as ving (“wing, subdivision of a squadron”) + leder (“leader”), literally “wing leader”. The aviation sense of ving is borrowed from English wing.
Compare English Wing leader, the exact structural and semantic equivalent. The Norwegian Armed Forces also uses Wing Leader as the English rendering of the Norwegian position; whether vingleder was directly modelled after the English expression is unclear.
